hints: Look closely at the shape of each polysaccharide. Which one is a straight chain and which two have side branches?
Enzyme X can only break alpha-1,4 bonds from the ends, so think about what happens when it reaches an alpha-1,6 branch point.
walkthrough:
**Recall the structure of the three polysaccharides**

All three are made of alpha-glucose joined by alpha-1,4-glycosidic bonds. The big difference is branching.

Amylose is unbranched, amylopectin is branched with alpha-1,6 bonds, and glycogen is very highly branched with many alpha-1,6 bonds.

**See what enzyme X can and cannot do**

Enzyme X works only from the ends and only breaks alpha-1,4 bonds to release maltose. It cannot break the alpha-1,6 bonds at branch points.

So every time it meets a branch, it gets stuck and leaves that part undigested.

**Rank from least to most completely hydrolysed**

Glycogen has the most branches, so it gets stuck most often and is least completely hydrolysed. Amylopectin has fewer branches, so it is hydrolysed more than glycogen. Amylose has no branches, so it can be broken down completely to maltose.

That gives the order: glycogen (least) to amylopectin to amylose (most), which is row D.

options.A: This is backwards. Amylose has no branches to stop the enzyme, so it is most, not least, completely hydrolysed.
options.B: Amylose is correctly least here, but glycogen is more branched than amylopectin, so glycogen cannot be hydrolysed more completely than amylopectin.
options.C: Glycogen as least is correct, but amylose should be most completely hydrolysed, not in the middle.
options.D: Correct. Glycogen has most alpha-1,6 branches so is stopped most, amylopectin is intermediate, and unbranched amylose is fully hydrolysed to maltose.
